For bread is ended in one way, a tunic in another, a field here and there in another. Bread, that it may be consumed and be no more. A tunic, that it may be completed and be perfect. 69_marg862: For the end of the commandment, etc. Augustine. For charity, by which we love God and neighbour, and which is the root of all good things, securely possesses the whole greatness and breadth of the divine words. Whence: on these two commandments dependeth the whole law and the prophets. If, then, you have no leisure to search all the sacred pages, to unroll all the volumes of discourses, to penetrate all the secrets of the Scriptures, hold fast charity, on which all things depend, because the end of all is the love of God and neighbour. No kind of things to be loved is passed over in these two commandments. For since the love of God comes first and the love of neighbour follows, nothing seems to be said of your love of yourself. But when it is said, “Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself,” the love of yourself by you is at the same time not passed over. Now he lives holily and justly who has an ordered love, so that he neither loves what is not to be loved, nor loves equally what is to be loved less or more, nor loves less or more what is to be loved equally. Every man, insofar as he is a sinner, is not to be loved; but insofar as he is a man, he is to be loved for God’s sake, and God for his own sake. And each ought to love God more than himself. Likewise another man is to be loved more than our body, because all these things are to be loved for God’s sake; another man can enjoy God with us, which the body cannot, because the body lives by the soul, by which we enjoy God. But all are to be loved equally, to equal goods; but since you cannot benefit all, counsel is to be given especially to those who, by the opportunities of places and times, or of any circumstances whatever, are joined to you more closely, as by a kind of lot. This, then, is the sum of all: that it be understood that the fullness of the law and of the divine Scriptures is charity, toward the thing which is to be enjoyed and the thing which can enjoy that thing with us, that is, God and neighbour; for it is commanded that God be loved and the neighbour, but that each love himself there is no need of another special commandment. The same: This charity is the love of God and of neighbour. The love of this world is called cupidity; cupidity is lessened as charity grows. Let cupidity, then, be restrained, and charity be stirred up.

69_marg877: That Christ Jesus came, etc. Christ had no cause for coming except to save sinners. Take away diseases, take away wounds, and there is no cause for medicine. But the great physician came from heaven; a great sick man lay throughout the whole globe of the earth. That sick man is the human race, which had wholly perished, since one man sinned, in whom was the whole. But one came without sin, to save from sin. For “the Son of man is come to seek and to save that which was lost”; he came by that in which he was man. For by that in which he was God, he was always here, he who said: “Do not I fill heaven and earth?” So he was both in the world and came into the world: he was here by his divine majesty, he came by human weakness. Why did he come? From mercy, namely because he willed to take away sins and save sinners. For not our merits but our sins drew him from heaven to earth; whence: “And thou shalt call his name Jesus.” Why? Hear: “For he shall save his people.” From what? “From their sins.” Do little children belong to this people? They plainly do. So believe, and with this faith bring little children to the grace of Christ. Why do you say to me: he is healthy, he has no fault? Why do you run with him to the physician, if he has no fault? If he were healthy, Jesus would not cry out: “Suffer the little children to come unto me,” etc.

69_marg901: This is that arbiter whom Job desires, saying: “Would that there were an arbitrator between us.” Augustine. It was fitting that a mediator between God and men should have something like God and something like men, lest, being like men in all things, he be far from God, or, being like God in all things, he be far from men, and so be no mediator. And so Christ, the true mediator, appeared between mortal sinners and the immortal just One: mortal with men, just with God. Therefore Christ is called mediator of God and men, because between God and mortal man there is God made man, reconciling man to God. He is mediator insofar as he is man. But insofar as he is the Word he is not in the middle, because he is equal to God, and God with God, and together one God. It was fitting that he neither fail to become mortal, nor remain mortal: made mortal indeed, not by the weakening of the Word’s divinity, but by taking on the weakness of flesh. But the good angels cannot be mediators between wretched mortals and the blessed immortal One, because they are blessed and immortal with God in such a way that they are not mortal or wretched with men. The evil angels, however, are in a way mediators, because they are immortal with God, wretched with men. But they are not true and good mediators, because the mediator who is immortal and wretched puts himself between so as not to allow us to pass over to blessed immortality. The good mediator is contrary to him, because he both willed to be mortal for a time and was able to remain blessed in eternity, and did not put himself between so as to forbid passing over to blessed immortality. But he put himself between, mortal and blessed, so that, our mortality having passed, he might make us immortal from dead, and blessed from wretched. One mediator, then, is evil, who separates friends; another good, who reconciles the enemies of Jesus Christ.

69_marg909: Augustine. Although the Apostle calls him a transgressor, in the likeness of Adam’s transgression, yet he denies that he was seduced; whence also, when questioned, he did not say: “The woman seduced me,” but “she gave me, and I did eat.” But the woman said: “The serpent deceived me.” This the Apostle properly called seduction, by which what was being urged, though false, was thought true, namely that God had forbidden them to touch that tree because he knew that if they touched it they would be as gods, as though he begrudged divinity to them, he who had made them men. But even if some desire of experiencing it, on account of some elation of mind (which could not be hidden from God, the searcher of inward things), stirred the man, when he saw that the woman had not died after taking that food, yet I do not think that he, if he was already endowed with a spiritual mind, in any way believed what the devil suggested. Therefore he says: Adam was not seduced first, nor in that in which the woman was, so as to believe that to be true: “You shall be as gods.” But he thought that both could be done: that he might gratify his wife and obtain pardon through penance. He therefore sinned less who thought of penance and of God’s mercy. For after the woman was seduced and ate, he ate what she gave him, so that he might eat with her; he did not wish to grieve her, whom he believed would pine away without his comfort and, estranged from him, perish altogether; not indeed from carnal craving for the food, which he had not yet felt, but from a certain friendly goodwill, by which it often happens that God is offended lest a friend be offended; which that he ought not to have done, the vengeance of the divine sentence showed. Therefore in some other way he too was deceived. For being inexperienced in the divine sentence he could be mistaken in this, that he believed what was committed to be venial. But by that serpentine guile by which the woman was seduced, I think he could in no way have been seduced.

69_marg912: If a man desire the office of a bishop, he desireth a good work. Jerome to Oceanus. Work: not dignity, but labour; not delights; not to grow in loftiness, but to grow less in humility, that he may become the servant and minister of men for Christ’s sake; that, leaving aside Rachel, fair of face, but not forsaking her, he may go in with Jacob to Lia, bleary-eyed. And that he may come down from the mountain with Moses to the plains, and from the leisure of contemplation to the labour of action. For no one ought to be so at leisure as not to think, even in that leisure, of his neighbour’s profit, nor so active as not to seek the contemplation of God. In leisure, idle rest ought not to delight, but either the inquiry into or the finding of truth, that each may advance in it and not envy another what he has found. In action, however, honour in this life or power is not to be loved, because all things are vanity under the sun, but the work itself which is done through honour and power, so that it is done rightly and profitably, namely so as to avail for the salvation of those under him. Whence: If a man desire the office of a bishop, he desireth a good work. He wished to explain what the episcopate is, because it is the name of a work, not of an honour; for it is a Greek word and the name is derived from this, that he who is set over those over whom he is set, oversees them, bearing the care of them. For scopos is intention, epi is over. Hence in Latin bishop is called “overseer,” that he may understand that he is not a bishop who has loved to preside, not to profit. For the episcopate is an intention over one’s own life and that of others. So no one is forbidden from the study of knowing the truth, which belongs to praiseworthy leisure. But the higher place, without which a people cannot be ruled, even if it is held and administered as is fitting, is sought unbecomingly. Therefore in leisure the profit of the neighbour is to be thought of; in action the contemplation of God is to be sought. The love of truth seeks holy leisure; the necessity of charity undertakes just business. If no one lays this burden on you, you must be free for truth. If it is laid on, it must be taken up because of the necessity of charity. But even so the delight of truth is not to be abandoned, lest that sweetness be withdrawn and this necessity overwhelm.

That is, those who are destitute of the help of all their own, and who cannot work with their own hands, whom poverty weakens and age wears out, whose hope is God and whose whole work is prayer. From this it is given to understand that young widows, except those whom infirmity excuses, are to be left to their own labour or to the service of their children and kinsfolk, and are not to be received. Honour, moreover, is here taken either for alms or for a gift, as in that: “Let the priests that rule well be esteemed worthy of double honour: especially they who labour in the word and doctrine.” And in the gospel the Lord explains the commandment of the law in which it is said: “Honour thy father,” that it ought to be understood not in the sound of words, since the want of parents can be mocked by empty flattery, but in supplying the necessaries of life. For when God commanded that children should feed their poor parents and repay to the old the benefits which as little ones they had received, the scribes and Pharisees on the contrary taught children not to entrust to their parents corban, that is, “the gift which I have promised to the altar and have vowed to the gifts of the temple; if you receive food from me, it will be turned to your refreshment”; and so it came about that, while father and mother were in need, the children offered a sacrifice, which the priests and scribes consumed.

He neither could nor can be changed by any turning, nor could nor will he be able to sin by any change. But when it is granted to any rational creature that it cannot sin, this is not properly of its nature, but of the grace of God. Those things that are against religion are not the other ones to be avoided; for some novelties of words agree with the teaching of religion, such as the very name Christian, of which it is written when it began to be spoken. For in Antioch, after the ascension of the Lord, they were first called Christians, as is read in the Acts of the Apostles. Also against the impiety of the Arians the Fathers handed down the new word homoousion, but by such a name they did not signify a new thing, for that is called homoousion which is of one and the same substance. For if every novelty were profane, it would not be said by the Lord: “A new commandment I give unto you,” nor would the Testament be called new, nor would the whole Church sing a new canticle.
